Use the supplied query-property assessment only as an uncertain physicochemical prior. It is not experimental evidence or a label prediction. The highest-transfer analogue (0.8157) shows only 24% brain penetration relative to plasma in rat, making it the strongest individual anchor because it combines the highest transfer score with a direct systemic brain-penetration measurement. Its structure contains an ionizable piperidine and several polar functionalities but is not an obvious extreme BBB non-penetrant. The experimental result therefore outweighs any more favorable physicochemical intuition: whatever mechanism limits its CNS exposure is real. Because the transfer score is high and the query shares relevant ionization and heteroatom features, that measured phenotype has strong implications for the query.

The next three analogues have closely matched transfer scores (0.7874, 0.7855, and 0.7800) and independently support the same direction. One is relatively lipophilic and contains a tertiary amine yet shows minimal CSF exposure after intravenous dosing; another combines aromatic hydrophobicity with a basic amine but exhibits very low brain uptake that increases markedly after ABC-transporter inhibition; the third has substantial aromatic surface yet gives CSF concentrations below 5% of plasma in humans. The pattern continues at 0.7708 and 0.7603, where biodistribution and brain-to-blood measurements again show poor CNS exposure. Both molecules retain substantial hydrophobic/aromatic character, demonstrating experimentally that lipophilicity alone does not ensure brain penetration when other liabilities such as ionization, polarity, size, or transporter recognition intervene.
